key_terms.meaning: Input → drive circuit → source (LED or laser) → fiber → photodetector (PIN or APD) → amplifier → output
Loss = α × L (α in dB/km, L in km); P<sub>out</sub>(dBm) = P<sub>in</sub>(dBm) − loss
sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁, measured from the normal at the core–cladding wall
Needs n₁ > n₂ and an angle of incidence above θ<sub>c</sub>; no power leaves the core
n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²), the half-angle of the cone of guided rays
NA = n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²) = n₁√(2Δ), dimensionless
Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²) ≈ (n₁ − n₂)/n₁
n₀ sin θ<sub>as</sub> cos γ = NA, so skew rays are accepted over a wider cone
V = (2πd/λ)√(n₁² − n₂²) with full thickness d; mode m guided for V > mπ; single-mode for V < π
A transverse field pattern that keeps its shape as it travels, with one propagation constant β
n(r) = n₁[1 − 2Δ(r/a)<sup>α</sup>]<sup>½</sup> for r < a; α = 2 is parabolic
V = (2πa/λ)·NA with core radius a
M ≈ V²/2 (step index), M ≈ V²/4 (parabolic graded index), at large V
V < 2.405, the LP₁₁ cutoff (first zero of J₀)
λ<sub>c</sub> = 2πa·NA/2.405; single-mode for λ > λ<sub>c</sub>
v<sub>p</sub> = ω/β = c/n<sub>eff</sub>
v<sub>g</sub> = dω/dβ = c/N<sub>g</sub>, N<sub>g</sub> = n<sub>eff</sub> − λ dn<sub>eff</sub>/dλ; delay τ = LN<sub>g</sub>/c
Solve the thickness slab for n<sub>eff,1</sub>, then a width slab with core n<sub>eff,1</sub>
λ<sub>B</sub> = 2n̄a with a one full period and n̄ the thickness-weighted mean index
A band of wavelengths with no propagating mode in a periodic dielectric

takeaways: A fiber link is a source, a glass guide and a detector; the glass removes the bandwidth, loss and interference limits of copper.
Light stays in the core by total internal reflection; sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁ at the wall and n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²) at the end face.
Numerical aperture is the one number that links the two indices to the launch cone; Δ says the same thing as a fraction, and NA = n₁√(2Δ).
Skew rays are accepted over a wider cone than meridional rays: sin θ<sub>as</sub> = NA/cos γ.
Maxwell's equations with boundary conditions allow only discrete field patterns, the modes; V decides how many a guide carries.
A step-index fiber carries about V²/2 modes, a parabolic graded-index fiber about V²/4, and the graded profile makes rays arrive together.
A fiber is single-mode only for V < 2.405, that is for wavelengths longer than λ<sub>c</sub> = 2πa·NA/2.405.
Bits travel at the group velocity c/N<sub>g</sub>, not at the phase velocity c/n<sub>eff</sub>; delay is τ = LN<sub>g</sub>/c.
Chip waveguides add sideways confinement to the slab; the effective index method checks both directions with the slab rule V < π.
A periodic dielectric reflects a band of wavelengths centred on λ<sub>B</sub> = 2n̄a, and defects in it guide or trap light.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the derivation of the acceptance angle and numerical aperture, the mode picture of a planar guide, the V number with the mode count and cutoff wavelength, and a comparison of fiber types; numerical parts carry the units at every step.

bank.q: Draw the block diagram of a general optical fiber communication system and explain the function of each block. List six advantages of optical fiber over copper cable, with one reason for each.
outline: Blocks: input, drive circuit, optical source (LED or laser), fiber with splices and connectors, photodetector (PIN or APD), amplifier and decision circuit, output
Source is the E/O converter, detector the O/E converter; the fiber guides light by total internal reflection
Advantages with reasons: bandwidth, low loss, EMI immunity, isolation, safety, size and weight, security, cheap raw material
A short dB loss check

svg.aria: Block diagram in a row: input, drive circuit, source, fiber cable, detector, amplifier and decision circuit, output.

answer: Input and drive circuit. The information arrives as an electrical signal: a bit stream (digital link) or a continuous waveform (analog link). The drive circuit turns it into a current suited to the source, including the bias that sets the operating point.

Optical source. An LED or a semiconductor laser turns the drive current into light whose power follows the current. This is the electrical-to-optical (E/O) conversion. LEDs are cheap and broad in spectrum and suit short multimode links; lasers give a narrow, powerful beam for single-mode and long-haul links.

Fiber channel. A silica core of index n₁ inside a cladding of lower index n₂ guides the light by total internal reflection. Lengths of fiber are joined by splices and connectors; long routes add optical amplifiers or regenerators. The channel attenuates the light (dB/km) and spreads pulses.
Photodetector. A PIN photodiode or an avalanche photodiode turns the arriving light into a current, the optical-to-electrical (O/E) conversion.

Amplifier and decision circuit. A low-noise amplifier raises the small photocurrent; a filter shapes it, and in a digital link a decision circuit, timed by a recovered clock, decides 1 or 0 in each bit slot. The result is the electrical output.

answer.text: Advantages over copper, each with its reason:

head: Advantage
Reason
rows: the optical carrier is about 1.94 × 10¹⁴ Hz at 1550 nm, and WDM puts many wavelengths on one fiber
silica is very transparent in the near infrared, so spans of tens of kilometres need no repeater
glass is a dielectric, so motors, power lines and lightning induce no noise in it
no metal joins the ends, so there are no ground loops or surge paths
no current and no spark, so fiber can run through fuel and chemical plants
a 125 µm glass fiber replaces bulky copper pairs of far lower capacity
nothing radiates, and a tap needs physical access and adds detectable loss
silica comes from sand; copper is costly

answer: Drawbacks worth one line: splicing and connectors need precision tools, the glass breaks if bent too tightly, and both ends need converters.

answer.text: Closing check with numbers. A 20 km span with 0.2 dB/km and a 1 mW (0 dBm) launch:
answer.pre:
loss = 0.2 dB/km × 20 km = 4 dB
P<sub>out</sub> = 0 dBm − 4 dB = −4 dBm = 1 mW × 10<sup>−0.4</sup> = 0.398 mW

answer: So 40 % of the launched light survives 20 km of fiber, which is why one fiber span can be tens of kilometres long.

bank.q: State the laws of reflection and refraction. Define the critical angle and derive its expression. Explain total internal reflection and the two conditions needed for it, with a ray diagram.
outline: Law of reflection; Snell's law n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂ with angles from the normal
Critical angle when θ₂ = 90°: sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁
TIR conditions: n₁ > n₂ and θ₁ > θ<sub>c</sub>; evanescent field in the cladding
Ray diagram with three rays; a numerical value of θ<sub>c</sub>
answer: Law of reflection. At a boundary the reflected ray lies in the plane of incidence and leaves at the same angle to the normal as the incident ray: θreflected = θincident.

Law of refraction (Snell's law). The refracted ray lies in the same plane and n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where θ₁ and θ₂ are measured from the normal in the media of index n₁ and n₂. The index n = c/v is larger in the medium where light is slower.
Going into a rarer medium. If n₁ > n₂ (core to cladding), sin θ₂ = (n₁/n₂) sin θ₁ is larger than sin θ₁, so the ray bends away from the normal and θ₂ > θ₁.

answer.text: Critical angle. As θ₁ grows, θ₂ reaches 90° first. The θ₁ at which this happens is the critical angle θc:
answer.pre:
n₁ sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂ sin 90° = n₂
sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁
θ<sub>c</sub> = sin⁻¹(n₂/n₁)

answer: Total internal reflection. For θ₁ > θc, Snell's law would need sin θ₂ > 1, which no real angle satisfies. No refracted ray exists and all the light is reflected back into the core. A weak evanescent field reaches a fraction of a wavelength into the cladding, but it carries no power away, so the reflection is complete.
The two conditions: (1) the light must travel from the higher index to the lower index (n₁ > n₂); (2) the angle of incidence, measured from the normal, must exceed θc.

answer: Closing check. The 60° ray in the diagram: sin θ₂ = 1.50 × sin 60°/1.45 = 1.50 × 0.8660/1.45 = 0.8959, so θ₂ = 63.6°, larger than 60°, bending away from the normal as expected. The small index step of a fiber gives a large θc (75.2°), so only rays travelling nearly along the axis are trapped.

bank.q: Define the numerical aperture of a step-index fiber and derive NA = √(n₁² − n₂²). Relate it to the acceptance angle and to the relative index difference Δ, and evaluate it for n₁ = 1.48, n₂ = 1.46.
outline: Definition NA = n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub>
Snell's law at the end face: n₀ sin θ₀ = n₁ sin θ<sub>r</sub>
The ray meets the wall at φ = 90° − θ<sub>r</sub>; TIR needs φ ≥ θ<sub>c</sub>
At the limit n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = n₁ cos θ<sub>c</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²)
NA = n₁√(2Δ) with Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²) ≈ (n₁ − n₂)/n₁; NA is dimensionless
Numbers: NA 0.2425, θ<sub>a</sub> 14.0°
answer: Set-up. A step-index fiber has core index n₁ and cladding index n₂ (n₁ > n₂); the end face is flat and perpendicular to the axis, in a medium of index n₀. A meridional ray enters at θ₀ to the axis, travels at θr to the axis in the core, and meets the core–cladding wall at angle φ to the wall's normal.
Snell's law at the end face. The axis is the normal to the end face, so n₀ sin θ₀ = n₁ sin θr.
Geometry at the wall. The wall is parallel to the axis, so its normal is perpendicular to the axis and φ = 90° − θr.
TIR condition. The ray is guided if φ ≥ θc, with sin θc = n₂/n₁. A larger θ₀ gives a larger θr and a smaller φ, so there is a largest θ₀, the acceptance angle θa, at which φ = θc exactly.

answer.text: Derivation at the limit (θ₀ = θa, θr = 90° − θc):
answer.pre:
n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = n₁ sin(90° − θ<sub>c</sub>) = n₁ cos θ<sub>c</sub>
         = n₁ √(1 − sin²θ<sub>c</sub>) = n₁ √(1 − n₂²/n₁²)
         = √(n₁² − n₂²)

answer: Definition. The numerical aperture is NA = n₀ sin θa, so NA = √(n₁² − n₂²). In air (n₀ = 1) θa = sin⁻¹(NA). NA is a pure number and depends only on the indices, not on the outside medium; the acceptance cone is the cone of half-angle θa about the axis.

answer.pre:
Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²)  ⇒  n₁² − n₂² = 2n₁²Δ  ⇒  NA = n₁√(2Δ)
for n₁ ≈ n₂:  n₁² − n₂² = (n₁ + n₂)(n₁ − n₂) ≈ 2n₁(n₁ − n₂), so Δ ≈ (n₁ − n₂)/n₁

answer: Outside medium. If the end face is in a liquid of index 1.33, sin θa = 0.2425/1.33 = 0.1823 and θa = 10.51°: the cone narrows, but NA = n₀ sin θa = 1.33 × 0.1823 = 0.2425 is unchanged, which is why NA, not θa, is quoted on data sheets.

Meaning. A larger NA collects more light from a broad source such as an LED, but it also raises the V number and the number of modes, so multimode pulse spreading grows; single-mode fibers use NA near 0.1.

Closing check. Inside the core the limiting ray travels at θr = sin⁻¹(0.2425/1.48) = sin⁻¹(0.1638) = 9.43°, and meets the wall at 90° − 9.43° = 80.57°, which is exactly θc. The derivation and the numbers agree.

bank.q: Explain the electromagnetic mode theory of a symmetric planar dielectric guide. Why does it support only discrete field patterns? Define mode number, cutoff and the V number, and apply them to a guide with n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48, d = 5 µm at λ = 1.3 µm.
outline: Wave equation in each layer, field e<sup>j(ωt − βz)</sup>
Oscillating in the core, evanescent in the cladding: k₀n₂ < β < k₀n₁
Continuity of tangential E and H gives tan(κd/2) = γ/κ (even) and −cot(κd/2) = γ/κ (odd): discrete β
TE and TM; mode number m = number of zeros; cutoff V = mπ
Numbers: V = 5.90, two TE modes, n<sub>eff</sub> 1.4969 and 1.4882
answer: The guide. A core of index n₁ and thickness d lies between two claddings of index n₂ < n₁. It is infinite in y, light travels along z, and the core occupies −d/2 < x < d/2.

answer.text: Wave equation. In each layer Maxwell's equations give ∇²E = μ₀ε₀n² ∂²E/∂t². With E = E(x) ej(ωt − βz):
answer.pre:
d²E/dx² + (k₀²n² − β²) E = 0,   k₀ = 2π/λ
core:     E'' + κ² E = 0,  κ² = k₀²n₁² − β²   (oscillates)
cladding: E'' − γ² E = 0,  γ² = β² − k₀²n₂²   (decays)

answer: Guided condition. To oscillate in the core and decay in the cladding, both κ and γ must be real: k₀n₂ < β < k₀n₁, so the effective index neff = β/k₀ lies between n₂ and n₁. β above k₀n₁ is impossible; β below k₀n₂ makes the field oscillate in the cladding too, so it radiates (a radiation mode).

answer.text: Why discrete. Inside, E = A cos κx (even) or A sin κx (odd); outside, E = B e−γ(|x| − d/2). Tangential E and H (hence E and dE/dx for TE) must be continuous at x = ±d/2. Dividing slope by value:
answer.pre:
even modes:  tan(κd/2)  = γ/κ
odd modes:  −cot(κd/2) = γ/κ
with κ² + γ² = k₀²(n₁² − n₂²)  (fixed)

answer: Because κ and γ are tied together by the last line, these are transcendental equations with only a finite number of roots. Each root gives one allowed β and one field pattern: a mode, which keeps its shape as it travels.
TE and TM. TE modes have E only along y; TM modes have H only along y. Each family has its own roots; for a weak index step they nearly coincide.

Mode number and cutoff. The mode number m equals the number of zeros of the field across the core (TE₀ none, TE₁ one). A mode is at cutoff when β falls to k₀n₂ (γ = 0) and its field no longer decays. Setting γ = 0 gives κd = mπ with κ = k₀√(n₁² − n₂²).

answer.pre:
V = k₀ d √(n₁² − n₂²) = (2πd/λ) √(n₁² − n₂²)
mode m guided when V > mπ;  number of TE modes = floor(V/π) + 1
single-mode when V < π  (TE₀ has no cutoff)

answer.text: Numbers for n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48, d = 5 µm, λ = 1.3 µm:

answer: Field picture. TE₀ is a single cosine hump in the core with short exponential tails; TE₁ is one positive and one negative lobe with a zero at the centre and longer tails, because it is closer to cutoff. The higher the mode, the smaller β, the larger the zig-zag angle in ray terms, and the more power in the cladding.

Closing check. For TE₀, κ = 4.833 × √(2.25 − 1.4969²) = 0.466 µm⁻¹, so tan(κd/2) = tan(1.165) = 2.33, and γ/κ = 1.084/0.466 = 2.33: the eigenvalue equation is satisfied. TE₂ would need V > 2π = 6.28, and V = 5.90 is below that, so exactly two TE modes are guided.

bank.q: A step-index fiber has core index 1.50 and cladding index 1.48. Calculate the numerical aperture, the acceptance angle in air, the critical angle at the core–cladding boundary and the relative index difference. Find also the acceptance angle when the fiber end is in water (n₀ = 1.33).
outline: Δ = 0.01324 exact, 0.01333 approximate
In water sin θ<sub>a</sub> = 0.2441/1.33, θ<sub>a</sub> = 10.57°
NA dimensionless; θ<sub>a</sub> from the axis, θ<sub>c</sub> from the normal
answer: Given: n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.48, air outside (n₀ = 1), then water (n₀ = 1.33).
Acceptance angle in air. sin θa = NA/n₀ = 0.2441, so θa = sin⁻¹(0.2441) = 14.13°. The full acceptance cone is 2θa = 28.26° wide.
Critical angle. sin θc = n₂/n₁ = 1.48/1.50 = 0.98667, so θc = 80.63°, measured from the normal to the core–cladding wall.
Acceptance angle in water. NA does not change, but sin θa = NA/n₀ = 0.2441/1.33 = 0.1835, so θa = 10.57°: the cone is narrower in water.

Why the angles are so different. θc = 80.63° is large because the index step is small (1.48/1.50 is close to 1): only rays travelling within 90° − 80.63° = 9.37° of the axis inside the core are trapped. Refraction at the end face opens that 9.37° out to 14.13° in air, because n₁ sin 9.37° = 1.50 × 0.1627 = 0.2441 = sin 14.13°.

Effect on coupling. A source whose light spreads wider than the cone loses the rest. For an LED radiating as a Lambertian source into air, the fraction of its power inside a cone of half-angle θa is sin²θa = NA² = 0.2441² = 0.0596, about 6 %, which is why LEDs couple poorly into fibers of small NA (see Source-to-fiber power launching and coupling).

A ray launched at 16° from air is outside the cone: inside, sin θr = sin 16°/1.50 = 0.2756/1.50 = 0.1838, θr = 10.59°, and it meets the wall at 90° − 10.59° = 79.41°, below θc = 80.63°, so part of it refracts into the cladding at every reflection and it is soon lost.

Closing check. The ray launched at 14.13° in air travels inside at sin⁻¹(0.2441/1.50) = sin⁻¹(0.1627) = 9.37° to the axis, and meets the wall at 90° − 9.37° = 80.63° = θc. The acceptance angle and the critical angle are consistent.

bank.q: A multimode step-index fiber has core radius 25 µm and NA = 0.22, used at λ = 1300 nm. Find the V number and the approximate number of guided modes. Is the fiber single-mode? Repeat for λ = 850 nm, and give the mode counts if the fiber were parabolic graded-index with the same core and on-axis NA.
outline: V = 2πa·NA/λ with a and λ in the same unit
V > 2.405 at both: multimode; λ<sub>c</sub> = 14.4 µm
Graded index: M ≈ V²/4: 177 and 413
answer: Given: a = 25 µm, NA = 0.22, λ = 1.30 µm and 0.85 µm. Keep a and λ in µm so a/λ is a pure number.
Modes at 1300 nm. For a step-index fiber with large V, M ≈ V²/2 = 26.58²/2 = 706.6/2 = 353 modes.

Single-mode? Single-mode needs V < 2.405. Both 26.58 and 40.66 are far above it, so the fiber is multimode at both wavelengths. Its cutoff wavelength would be λc = 2πa·NA/2.405 = (157.08 × 0.22)/2.405 = 34.56/2.405 = 14.4 µm, far beyond any working window.

Graded-index version. With the same core radius and on-axis NA, V is unchanged, but a parabolic profile (α = 2) carries M ≈ V²/4: 706.6/4 = 177 modes at 1300 nm and 1652.9/4 = 413 at 850 nm. The general rule is M ≈ [α/(α + 2)]V²/2, which gives V²/2 as α → ∞.
Why the count rises at 850 nm. V is proportional to 1/λ and M to V², so M scales as 1/λ²: (1300/850)² = 2.339, and 353 × 2.339 = 826. A shorter wavelength sees a larger core in wavelength terms.

Note on the formulas. V²/2 and V²/4 are large-V estimates and count both polarizations; they are accurate to a few percent here because V is in the tens, but they fail near V = 2.405, where the LP modes must be counted one by one.

What the large mode count means. Each mode travels at a slightly different group velocity, so a pulse launched into hundreds of modes arrives spread out in time; that intermodal dispersion, not loss, usually limits a step-index multimode link. A graded profile with the same V halves the number of modes and, far more importantly, makes them arrive almost together.

answer.text: How small would the core have to be for single-mode operation at 1300 nm?

answer: A 2.26 µm radius with NA = 0.22 is impractically small to align, which is why single-mode fibers use a smaller NA (about 0.1) and a core radius near 4 to 4.5 µm instead.
Closing check. The ratio of the two V values is 40.66/26.58 = 1.530, equal to 1300/850 = 1.529, as V ∝ 1/λ requires.

bank.q: Explain how a graded-index profile reduces intermodal dispersion. A graded-index fiber has n₁ = 1.48 on the axis, n₂ = 1.46 in the cladding, core radius 25 µm and profile parameter α = 2. Tabulate its index profile, find its on-axis NA, and compare its modal delay spread per kilometre with a step-index fiber of the same indices.
outline: n(r) = n₁[1 − 2Δ(r/a)<sup>α</sup>]<sup>½</sup> for r < a, n₂ outside; exact Δ = 0.01342
Profile: 1.48 on the axis falling to 1.46 at r = a
Off-axis rays travel longer paths but faster, so arrival times equalise; α ≈ 2 is near optimum
Step δτ/L = n₁Δ/c = 66.2 ns/km; parabolic δτ/L = n₁Δ²/(8c) = 111 ps/km; ratio 8/Δ ≈ 596
Graded multimode gives far higher bandwidth for the same core
answer: The problem in a step-index fiber. All rays travel at c/n₁, but a ray at a steep angle zig-zags over a longer path than the axial ray, so it arrives later. The spread of arrival times between the slowest and fastest rays is the intermodal (modal) delay spread; it widens every pulse and limits the bit rate.

The graded-index idea. Make the index highest on the axis and lower towards the core edge. Light is faster where the index is lower (v = c/n). A ray that swings far from the axis travels a longer path, but most of it lies in faster, lower-index glass; the axial ray takes the shortest path through the slowest glass. With the right profile the two effects cancel almost exactly, and all rays arrive together.

Ray paths. Because the index falls continuously, a ray bends gradually back towards the axis instead of reflecting at a wall; it follows a smooth, nearly sinusoidal path crossing the axis periodically. Rays launched at different angles have nearly the same axial period in a parabolic profile.

On-axis NA. NA(0) = √(n₁² − n₂²) = √0.0588 = 0.2425; the local NA √(n(r)² − n₂²) falls to 0.222 at r = 10 µm and to zero at r = a, which is why a graded fiber carries about half as many modes as a step fiber with the same a and NA.

answer.text: Delay spread per kilometre (the formulas are derived with intermodal dispersion in signal degradation; used here only for comparison):

answer: Consequence. A pulse spread of 66 ns per kilometre limits a 1 km step-index link to a few megabits per second, while about 0.11 ns per kilometre allows hundreds of megabits per second or more over the same kilometre. That is why multimode links in buildings use graded-index fiber.
Optimum profile. The cancellation is best for α close to 2 (slightly less than 2 once material dispersion is included); a profile far from the optimum leaves much of the step-index spread.
Closing check. At r = a the profile gives 1.48 × √(1 − 0.02684) = 1.48 × 0.98649 = 1.4600 = n₂, so the exact Δ makes the core meet the cladding without a step, as a graded profile must.

bank.q: A 10 km link uses fiber whose mode has group index 1.47 and effective index 1.45. Find the phase velocity, the group velocity, the pulse delay and the lag of the envelope behind the crests. Distinguish clearly between phase velocity and group velocity.
outline: v<sub>p</sub> = c/n<sub>eff</sub> = 2.069 × 10⁸ m/s
v<sub>g</sub> = c/N<sub>g</sub> = 2.041 × 10⁸ m/s
τ = L/v<sub>g</sub> = 49.0 µs; crest time 48.33 µs; lag 0.67 µs
Phase velocity ω/β: speed of a crest; group velocity dω/dβ: speed of the envelope, which carries the information
N<sub>g</sub> = n<sub>eff</sub> − λ dn<sub>eff</sub>/dλ
answer: Phase velocity. A single-frequency wave ej(ωt − βz) has crests where ωt − βz is constant, so a crest moves at vp = ω/β = c/neff. A pure single frequency carries no information.

Group velocity. A pulse contains a band of frequencies. Its envelope sits where these components add in phase, and that point moves at vg = dω/dβ = c/Ng, with Ng = neff − λ dneff/dλ. Bits, delay and timing follow vg. In silica the slope dneff/dλ is negative, so Ng > neff and the envelope is slower than the crests, which slide forward through it.
Delay per kilometre. τ/L = Ng/c = 1.47/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 4.90 µs/km, a figure used in timing and latency budgets.

Where Ng comes from. With β = 2πneff/λ, 1/vg = dβ/dω = (1/c)(neff − λ dneff/dλ). Here Ng − neff = 0.02 = −λ dneff/dλ, so at λ = 1.55 µm the slope would be dneff/dλ = −0.02/1.55 = −0.0129 per µm, a typical value for silica fiber.

Why the distinction matters. A rise-time or latency budget that used vp would put the pulse at the receiver 0.67 µs too early over 10 km, and 67 µs too early over 1000 km. Pulse spreading also comes from the group velocity: if Ng differs between the wavelengths in a pulse, they arrive at different times (chromatic dispersion).
Closing check. The lag equals L(Ng − neff)/c = 10⁴ × 0.02/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 6.7 × 10⁻⁷ s = 0.67 µs, the same as the difference of the two transit times.

bank.q: A step-index fiber has a cutoff wavelength of 1.20 µm. Explain what happens when it is used at 850 nm and at 1550 nm, supporting the answer with the V number and the meaning of 2.405. Which LP modes travel at 850 nm?
outline: λ<sub>c</sub> = 2πa·NA/2.405, so V = 2.405 λ<sub>c</sub>/λ
850 nm: V = 3.40 > 2.405: LP₀₁ and LP₁₁ (below 3.832)
1550 nm: V = 1.86 < 2.405: single-mode, LP₀₁ only
2.405 is the first zero of J₀, the LP₁₁ cutoff
Too small a V weakens confinement and raises bend loss
answer: V in terms of the cutoff. V = 2πa·NA/λ and, at cutoff, 2.405 = 2πa·NA/λc. Dividing, V = 2.405 λc/λ. So a and NA need not be known.

Meaning of 2.405. In a weakly guiding step-index fiber the LP₁₁ mode reaches cutoff at the first zero of the Bessel function J₀, V = 2.405. The fundamental LP₀₁ has no cutoff. So V < 2.405 means only LP₀₁ is guided (single-mode); V > 2.405 means LP₁₁ is guided too.

3.40 > 2.405, so the fiber is multimode at 850 nm. The next cutoff, for LP₂₁ and LP₀₂, is the first zero of J₁ at V = 3.832; 3.40 is below it, so exactly two LP mode groups travel: LP₀₁ and LP₁₁. They travel at different group velocities (intermodal dispersion) and their interference at the receiver gives modal noise.
1.86 < 2.405, so only LP₀₁ travels: single-mode operation with no intermodal dispersion. The same holds at 1310 nm, where V = 2.886/1.31 = 2.20.

Why 2.405 and not another number. In the weakly guiding fiber the LP₁₁ field in the core varies as J₁(ur/a); at cutoff the cladding decay constant goes to zero, and the matching condition reduces to J₀(V) = 0. The first zero of J₀ is 2.405, so LP₁₁ exists only for V > 2.405. LP₀₁'s condition at cutoff is J₁(V) = 0 with root V = 0, so it is always guided.

Number of modes at 850 nm. LP₀₁ has 2 field patterns (two polarizations) and LP₁₁ has 4 (two orientations, two polarizations), so 6 patterns travel. The large-V estimate V²/2 = 3.40²/2 = 5.8 happens to agree here, but near cutoff the exact count must be used.

Practical note. As V falls, the LP₀₁ field spreads further into the cladding (the mode field diameter grows) and the mode is held more weakly, so bend loss rises. That is why λc is kept only moderately below the working window instead of far below it.
Closing check. The fiber is single-mode for every λ > λc = 1.20 µm and multimode below it; 0.85 µm is below and 1.55 µm above, matching the V values 3.40 and 1.86.

bank.q: Compare step-index multimode, graded-index multimode and single-mode fibers on core size, NA, modes, intermodal dispersion, sources, connectors and cost. Recommend one type for a 300 m campus LAN and one for an 80 km trunk link, giving reasons.
outline: Table of core diameter, NA, V and mode count, dispersion, source, connector tolerance
Intermodal spread: step n₁Δ/c, graded n₁Δ²/(8c), single-mode none
Campus LAN: graded-index multimode with VCSEL or LED sources
Trunk: single-mode at 1550 nm with a laser
Cost per connector against cost per kilometre

answer.text: Dispersion in numbers. For n₁ = 1.48 and Δ = 0.01, the ideal intermodal spreads are:
answer.pre:
step index:  n₁Δ/c       = 1.48 × 0.01/(3 × 10⁸)       = 49.3 ns/km
parabolic:   n₁Δ²/(8c)   = 1.48 × 0.0001/(8 × 3 × 10⁸) = 61.7 ps/km
single-mode: no intermodal spread (only chromatic dispersion)

answer: Why each behaves so. A step-index multimode fiber has a large core and NA, so it collects light easily but its steep rays arrive late. A graded profile equalises the transit times, cutting the spread by a factor 8/Δ (800 here). A single-mode fiber has V < 2.405, so only LP₀₁ exists and there is nothing to spread between.

Sources and connectors. A large core and NA accept the broad beam of an LED and forgive a few micrometres of misalignment, so multimode connectors are cheap and quick to fit. A 9 µm single-mode core needs a laser and connectors aligned to about a micrometre, which costs more per joint.

Campus LAN, 300 m: choose graded-index multimode (50 µm). Over 300 m its ideal intermodal spread is about 0.3 × 61.7 = 19 ps, small enough for gigabit and faster links, and it works with low-cost VCSEL transceivers and quick-fit connectors. A LAN has many short runs and many connectors, so the low cost per connector and per transceiver dominates. Step-index multimode would spread pulses by about 15 ns over 300 m, too much for high rates.

Trunk, 80 km: choose single-mode fiber at 1550 nm. There is no intermodal dispersion, the loss is lowest at 1550 nm, so an 80 km span fits a power budget without a repeater, and the remaining chromatic dispersion can be managed. Multimode fiber is ruled out: even the graded spread would be 80 × 61.7 ps ≈ 4.9 ns, and its loss is higher.

Cost argument. On a trunk the cost per kilometre of cable and the number of repeaters dominate, so the dearer laser and connectors at the two ends are worth it. In a campus the cost of many transceivers and connectors dominates, so cheap multimode optics win over short lengths.

Mode counts for typical fibers at 850 nm. A 50 µm graded fiber with NA = 0.2 has V = (2π × 25/0.85) × 0.2 = 36.96 and about V²/4 = 341 modes; a 100 µm step fiber with NA = 0.3 has V = (2π × 50/0.85) × 0.3 = 110.9 and about V²/2 = 6147 modes; a single-mode fiber at 1310 nm has V below 2.405 and one mode.

Other points of comparison. Single-mode fiber has the lowest loss and is the only type used in the 1550 nm window with optical amplifiers. Multimode fiber's large core makes field splicing and testing easier and tolerates dust and misalignment better. Step-index multimode, including plastic fiber, survives where cost and ruggedness matter more than speed: short industrial and car links.
Closing check. The ratio of the step and parabolic spreads is 49.3 ns / 61.7 ps = 800 = 8/Δ = 8/0.01, consistent with the two formulas.

bank.q: A step-index fiber has n₁ = 1.46, Δ = 0.003 and core radius 4.5 µm. (a) Find n₂, NA, the acceptance angle and the critical angle. (b) Find the cutoff wavelength and V at 1310 and 1550 nm. (c) Evaluate whether it can serve a single-mode link in both windows, and if not, the largest core radius that would. (d) For contrast, a fiber with the same n₁, Δ = 0.01 and a = 25 µm is used at 850 nm: find V and the mode count.
outline: Multimode at 1310 nm (just), single-mode at 1550 nm; a < 4.26 µm for λ<sub>c</sub> ≤ 1.26 µm
Second fiber: NA = 0.2065, V = 38.2, M ≈ 728 (step)

answer.text: (a) Indices and angles. With the exact Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²):

answer: A single-mode fiber has a small NA, so its acceptance cone is narrow (6.5°) and rays must run almost along the axis (they meet the wall above 85.6°). This is why a laser, not an LED, is needed to launch into it.

The cutoff, 1.330 µm, lies above 1310 nm, so at 1310 nm the fiber carries LP₁₁ as well and is not single-mode; at 1550 nm it is single-mode. It cannot serve a link that must be single-mode in both windows.

answer.text: Redesign. Keep n₁ and Δ (so NA = 0.1131) and require λc ≤ 1.26 µm, leaving margin below 1310 nm:

answer: So the core radius must be cut from 4.5 µm to about 4.2 µm (core diameter about 8.4 µm). With a = 4.2 µm, V(1310 nm) = 2π × 4.2 × 0.1131/1.31 = 2.278 and V(1550 nm) = 1.93, both below 2.405. Lowering Δ instead would also work but weakens confinement and raises bend loss.

The multimode fiber has about twice the NA (θ<sub>a</sub> = 11.9°) and over five times the core radius, so it guides about 728 modes at 850 nm, against one in the redesigned single-mode fiber at 1310 or 1550 nm.

Practical judgement. A cutoff only 20 nm above the 1310 nm window (1.330 against 1.310 µm) is a borderline design: the LP₁₁ mode just above its cutoff is weakly guided and is lost in a few metres of cabled, bent fiber, so in practice the fiber may behave as single-mode at 1310 nm over long lengths. A design exam answer should not rely on that; it should place λc clearly below the window, as the redesign does.

Light gathering. The redesigned fiber keeps NA = 0.1131, so its acceptance cone stays at 6.49°: a laser with a narrow beam is still needed. The multimode fiber, with NA = 0.2065, accepts a cone of 11.9° and an LED can launch into it, but its 728 modes rule it out for long, fast links.
Closing check. For the original fiber, λc/λ = 1.330/1.31 = 1.015 and 2.405 × 1.015 = 2.44 = V(1310 nm), consistent with V = 2.405 λc/λ.

bank.q: Describe photonic crystals and the photonic band gap. Design a quarter-wave silicon nitride/silica mirror for 1550 nm and find its stop band. Contrast index guiding with band-gap guiding, and explain how a photonic crystal fiber and a photonic crystal waveguide use these ideas.
outline: Periodic dielectric with period near λ; Bragg reflection from every period
Band gap: wavelengths with no propagating mode; from periodicity, not absorption
Quarter-wave stack: d<sub>H</sub> = 193.8 nm, d<sub>L</sub> = 267.2 nm, a = 461.0 nm, λ<sub>B</sub> = 2n̄a = 1550 nm, band 1407–1726 nm
Defects create states in the gap: line-defect waveguides and point-defect cavities
Index-guiding PCF (solid core, modified TIR) against band-gap PCF (hollow core)
answer: Photonic crystal. A dielectric whose refractive index repeats in one, two or three dimensions with a period a comparable to the wavelength. Light is partly reflected at every boundary; at certain wavelengths the reflections from successive periods return in phase and add.

Photonic band gap. For a band of wavelengths around the Bragg condition, no wave can propagate through the periodic medium: the field decays from period to period and the light is reflected. The gap comes from the periodicity alone, not from absorption, much as the periodic lattice of a crystal makes an electronic band gap for electrons.

answer.text: Quarter-wave mirror for 1550 nm with nH = 2.0 (silicon nitride) and nL = 1.45 (silica):

answer: Defects. Breaking the period creates an allowed state inside the gap. A missing row of holes in a 2D crystal is a line defect: light at a gap wavelength cannot enter the crystal on either side, so it is guided along the line, even round 60° or 90° bends of a few micrometres. A missing hole is a point defect, a microcavity that stores light for many cycles in about a cubic wavelength; it is used for filters and tiny lasers.

Index guiding. The core has a higher index than the cladding and light is held by total internal reflection. An index-guiding photonic crystal fiber has a solid glass core inside a cladding of air holes; the holes lower the cladding's average index, so a modified TIR guides the light. Hole size and spacing set the mode area and dispersion, and some designs stay single-mode over a very wide band.

Band-gap guiding. The cladding is a photonic crystal whose gap forbids light at the working wavelength, so light is trapped in a core of lower index than the cladding, even air. A hollow-core band-gap fiber guides light mostly in air, giving low nonlinearity, high power handling and lower latency, which TIR cannot do.

Photonic crystal waveguide on a chip. A line defect in a silicon slab with a lattice of air holes: in-plane light is held by the gap, vertical light by TIR in the slab. Its strength is sharp bends and slow light (large group index) in a small area.

Evaluation. Band-gap structures give compact mirrors, cavities and bends that ordinary TIR guides cannot, but they demand nanometre accuracy (a 1550 nm gap needs a period near 460 to 520 nm), suffer scattering from rough holes, and work only inside the gap.
Closing check. The plain mean (2.0 + 1.45)/2 = 1.725 would put λB at 2 × 1.725 × 461.0 = 1590 nm; only the thickness-weighted n̄ = 1.681 gives the design wavelength 1550 nm.

bank.q: Explain strip, ridge and channel waveguides used in integrated optics. Why is light confined in two dimensions, and how is a single-mode guide designed? Use a buried guide 0.5 µm thick and 2 µm wide with n₁ = 1.50, n₂ = 1.45 at 1.55 µm. What difficulties appear when the guide is made very small?
outline: Strip: etched core; ridge: partly etched; channel: buried core
Vertical confinement by the layer stack, lateral by the side index step
Effective index method: thickness slab V = 0.778 → n<sub>eff,1</sub> = 1.4564; width slab V<sub>w</sub> = 1.11 < π
Single-mode up to about 5.7 µm width
Difficulties: sidewall scattering, fiber coupling loss, polarization dependence
answer: Types. A strip guide is a core layer etched into a strip on the substrate, covered by air or a deposited cladding. A ridge (rib) guide is only partly etched, leaving thin slabs at the sides that weaken lateral confinement. A channel (buried) guide has a rectangular core surrounded by cladding on all sides, made by diffusion, ion exchange or deposition. Some books use 'channel waveguide' for all of these.

Two-dimensional confinement. A planar slab holds light only across its thickness. Cutting the core to a finite width adds an index step at each side, so light is held vertically by the layer stack and sideways by the strip edges, and can be routed round a chip.

answer.text: Thickness check (slab V with full thickness t):

answer: The stack is symmetric, so V < π means one mode across the thickness; solving the slab gives n<sub>eff,1</sub> = 1.4564.

answer.text: Width check by the effective index method. Treat the guide from above as a slab of width w with core index neff,1 and side index n₂:

answer: Both checks pass, so the guide is single-mode, with effective index about 1.451. The lateral contrast (0.136) is much weaker than the material contrast (0.384), which is why the guide can be four times wider than thick and still single-mode.

Design steps. Choose the index contrast (sets bend radius and mode size); choose t so the vertical V is below π; find neff,1; choose w so the lateral V is below π; confirm with a numerical mode solver, because the effective index method is an estimate.

Difficulties when the guide is small. (1) Sidewall roughness from etching scatters light, and loss rises as the mode presses harder on the walls of a small, high-contrast core. (2) The chip's mode is far smaller than a fiber's (about 10 µm), so butt coupling loses much light unless tapers or grating couplers are used. (3) A thin, wide guide treats TE and TM differently, so the device becomes polarization dependent. (4) Small dimension errors shift neff and detune filters and interferometers.
Closing check. The guide index 1.4514 lies between n₂ = 1.45 and neff,1 = 1.4564, as each added confinement must lower neff.

bank.q: Explain how a skew ray differs from a meridional ray, derive or state the acceptance condition for skew rays, and show with numbers for a fiber of NA = 0.2425 why skew rays are accepted over a wider cone. What practical effects follow in a multimode fiber?
outline: Meridional: in a plane through the axis, crosses it; skew: never crosses it, helical path
Skew acceptance n₀ sin θ<sub>as</sub> cos γ = NA, so θ<sub>as</sub> ≥ θ<sub>a</sub>
Effects: more light collected from broad sources, measured NA larger over short lengths, longer paths add to modal spread
answer: Meridional ray. It lies in a plane that contains the fiber axis; seen end-on it runs along a diameter, crossing the axis between reflections. Its acceptance condition is n₀ sin θa = NA.

Skew ray. It enters off-axis and never crosses the axis. Seen end-on it traces a polygon of chords inside the core, each touching an inner circle; along the fiber it follows a helix. Two angles describe it: θ, its angle to the axis, and γ, the angle between its end-on projection and the core radius at the point of reflection. A meridional ray has γ = 0.

Constant reflection angle. In a straight, uniform step-index fiber every chord of a given skew ray is the same length and meets the wall at the same angle, so if the first reflection satisfies TIR, every reflection does.

answer.text: Acceptance condition. The direction cosine of the ray along the wall's normal is sin θr cos γ (θr inside the core), so TIR needs n₁ sin θr cos γ ≤ n₁ cos θc = √(n₁² − n₂²). With Snell's law at the end face, n₀ sin θ = n₁ sin θr:
answer.pre:
n₀ sin θ<sub>as</sub> · cos γ = √(n₁² − n₂²) = NA
sin θ<sub>as</sub> = NA / cos γ  ≥  NA = sin θ<sub>a</sub>

answer: So the more a ray is skewed, the wider the cone over which it is accepted; near grazing incidence on the wall (γ close to 90°) skew rays are trapped at any launch angle, though such rays are few and often leaky.

Practical effects. (1) A broad source such as an LED, or an off-axis launch, puts much power into skew rays, so a multimode fiber collects a little more light than the meridional NA predicts. (2) A far-field NA measured on a short length can come out larger than √(n₁² − n₂²), because skew and leaky rays leave at wider angles before they have been lost. (3) Skew rays follow longer helical paths, so they add to the spread of arrival times in multimode fiber. (4) Skew rays near the edge of the cone are hard to strip; test launches use mode scramblers and mandrel wraps to set a known launch.
Closing check. At γ = 45° the skew ray's normal component is sin θas cos γ = 0.3429 × 0.7071 = 0.2425 = NA, exactly the meridional limit, which confirms the condition.

glossary.def: The central, higher-index region of a fiber that carries the light.
The lower-index glass around the core that makes total internal reflection possible.
The plastic layer outside the cladding that protects the glass; it carries no light.
n = c/v, the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the material.
The angle of incidence at which the refracted ray grazes the boundary; sin θ<sub>c</sub> = n₂/n₁.
Complete reflection of light going into a lower-index medium at an angle of incidence above the critical angle.
The part of a guided field that decays exponentially into the cladding and carries no power away.
The largest launch angle, from the axis, at which a meridional ray is guided.
NA = n₀ sin θ<sub>a</sub> = √(n₁² − n₂²); a dimensionless measure of light-gathering power.
Δ = (n₁² − n₂²)/(2n₁²), about 0.003 for single-mode and 0.01 to 0.02 for multimode fiber.
A ray that lies in a plane containing the fiber axis and crosses the axis.
A ray that never crosses the axis and follows a helical path; it is accepted over a wider cone.
A field pattern that satisfies Maxwell's equations and the boundary conditions and keeps its shape as it travels.
β, the phase change per metre of a mode along the guide, in rad/m.
n<sub>eff</sub> = β/k₀; it lies between the cladding and core indices.
The fraction of a mode's power that travels inside the core.
The normalized frequency; for a fiber V = (2πa/λ)·NA, for a slab V = (2πd/λ)·NA.
A linearly polarized mode, the label used for weakly guiding fibers, such as LP₀₁ and LP₁₁.
A fiber with a constant core index and a sudden drop to the cladding index.
A fiber whose core index falls smoothly from the axis to the cladding.
The wavelength above which a fiber is single-mode; λ<sub>c</sub> = 2πa·NA/2.405.
The diameter at which the intensity of the fundamental mode falls to 1/e² of its peak.
v<sub>p</sub> = ω/β, the speed of a crest.
v<sub>g</sub> = dω/dβ = c/N<sub>g</sub>, the speed of a pulse envelope.
N<sub>g</sub> = n<sub>eff</sub> − λ dn<sub>eff</sub>/dλ.
A guide that confines light in both transverse directions; in some books only the buried kind.
A dielectric whose index repeats with a period comparable to the wavelength.
A band of wavelengths that cannot propagate through a photonic crystal.
